newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Interest rate cap derails Vietnam T-note sales.
newsitem.headline: Interest rate cap derails Vietnam T-note sales.

text.p: The State Bank of Vietnam has failed to allocate its targeted volume of Treasury paper in three auctions over the past month because the government is keeping a cap on interest rates, banking sources said on Wednesday.
Earlier on Wednesday the central State Bank allotted 2.9 billion dong ($262,000) worth of one-year Treasury notes to domestic institutions, far less than the 50 billion it had said was on offer.
The same problem occurred at the two previous auctions, when a total of 120 billion dong was offered but just 41 billion sold.

A State Bank official said many bidders were not allocated notes because bids above 8.00 percent on Wednesday and 7.89 percent in the two previous tenders were not accepted. He said banks had bid for stock at rates of up to 10 percent.
"It's all down to the interest rate," said one treasury dealer at a European bank in Ho Chi Minh City.
"The rate is decided by the Ministry of Finance beforehand and if bidders go below that rate, they get stock -- if they don't, they get none."
Bankers said that by cutting off bids to engineer low rates the authorities risked denting confidence in their plans for a more sophisticated money market in the future.
"These auctions are getting to be a joke," said one. "If they want to issue debt at a certain rate, why don't they just issue a domestic bond?"

Interest rates dropped sharply earlier this year, largely due to a dong surplus in the banking system. At the first sale of the year, on March 1, six-month bills were allotted at a rate of 15.00 percent.
The government, despite opposition from commercial banks, has been keen to see interest rates move down to stimulate borrowing and, in turn, the economy.
It is also anxious to narrow the gap between dong and dollar rates, currently about 6.5 percentage points, to encourage borrowing in the local currency.

However, speculation the government was preparing to sanction a dong devaluation to help narrow a yawning trade gap pushed the local currency slightly lower last month. That drained liquidity from the market and put upward pressure on rates.
Finance Minister Nguyen Sinh Hung said earlier this month that a devaluation was not being considered.
The dong was quoted at 11,068/11,078 per dollar on Wednesday compared with the level of around 11,000 at which it has traded since 1994.
